lead: A reinforced concrete beam can fail in three ways. The tension steel may yield first and the beam bends and warns before collapse. The concrete may crush first in a sudden brittle failure. Or steel and concrete may reach their limits together. The amount of tension steel relative to the balanced steel decides which mode occurs. Designers use this classification to keep beams ductile, so a warning comes before failure. The same idea appears in every singly reinforced beam check and in the design aids for flexure.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 and the stress–strain curves of Unit 1.

sections.h3: Neutral axis and the three modes

blocks.text: Let b be the width and d the effective depth of a rectangular beam. Let x<sub>u</sub> be the depth of the neutral axis from the extreme compression fibre. Concrete crushes at the ultimate strain ε<sub>cu</sub> = 0.0035. Plane sections remain plane, so the steel strain ε<sub>s</sub> follows from strain compatibility:

blocks.where: ε<sub>s</sub> is the tensile strain in the steel; ε<sub>cu</sub> is the concrete ultimate strain, 0.0035; d is the effective depth; x<sub>u</sub> is the neutral axis depth.

blocks.text: A smaller x<sub>u</sub> puts the steel farther from the neutral axis in strain terms and raises ε<sub>s</sub>. Steel yields when ε<sub>s</sub> reaches ε<sub>y</sub> = f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub>, where f<sub>y</sub> is the yield strength and E<sub>s</sub> = 200000 N/mm² is Young's modulus of steel.

The limiting neutral axis depth x<sub>u,max</sub> is the depth at which concrete crushing and steel yielding occur together. IS 456 gives x<sub>u,max</sub>/d = 0.53 for Fe250, 0.48 for Fe415 and 0.46 for Fe500. These values come from ε<sub>cu</sub> = 0.0035 paired with the code limiting steel strain ε<sub>s,lim</sub> = 0.002 + 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub>, which is slightly above the yield strain f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub>; at x<sub>u</sub> = x<sub>u,max</sub> the steel has already yielded.

If x<sub>u</sub> < x<sub>u,max</sub>, the steel yields before the concrete crushes. This is an under-reinforced section. If x<sub>u</sub> = x<sub>u,max</sub>, both happen together. This is a balanced section. If x<sub>u</sub> > x<sub>u,max</sub>, the concrete crushes before the steel yields. This is an over-reinforced section.
Some syllabi call these tension-controlled, balanced and compression-controlled sections. The names change; the comparison x<sub>u</sub> against x<sub>u,max</sub> does not.
At the balanced condition, concrete compression equals steel tension:

blocks.where: f<sub>ck</sub> is the characteristic concrete strength in N/mm²; f<sub>y</sub> is the steel yield strength in N/mm²; b is the beam width in mm; x<sub>u,max</sub> is the limiting neutral axis depth in mm; A<sub>st,lim</sub> is the balanced tension steel area in mm².

blocks.text: The factor 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> is the design average stress over the rectangular compression block. The factor 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> is the design tensile stress in steel. Solve for the balanced steel area and the limiting steel percentage:

blocks.where: A<sub>st,lim</sub> is the balanced steel area in mm²; other symbols are as defined above.
p<sub>t,lim</sub> is the limiting steel percentage; d is the effective depth in mm.

blocks.text: A provided percentage p<sub>t</sub> = 100 A<sub>st</sub>/(b d) below p<sub>t,lim</sub> means A<sub>st</sub> < A<sub>st,lim</sub>, so the section is under-reinforced. A value above p<sub>t,lim</sub> means over-reinforced. Values for f<sub>ck</sub> = 30 N/mm²:
The values depend on f<sub>y</sub> because x<sub>u,max</sub>/d depends on f<sub>y</sub>. Do not use the Fe415 row for Fe500 steel.

items: Read b, d, f<sub>ck</sub>, f<sub>y</sub> and A<sub>st</sub>.
Pick x<sub>u,max</sub>/d for the actual f<sub>y</sub>.
Compute A<sub>st,lim</sub> from the balanced force equation.
Compare. If A<sub>st</sub> < A<sub>st,lim</sub> or p<sub>t</sub> < p<sub>t,lim</sub>, under-reinforced; equal, balanced; greater, over-reinforced.

blocks.text: The comparison is about the neutral axis, not about A<sub>st</sub> alone. A beam with 800 mm² of steel can be under-reinforced in a large section and over-reinforced in a very small one. Always compare with A<sub>st,lim</sub> for the same b, d, f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>y</sub>.

In a real check, the strain diagram gives x<sub>u</sub>. For an under-reinforced section, steel has yielded, so the tension force is 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>st</sub> and x<sub>u</sub> follows from 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub>b x<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>st</sub>. For an over-reinforced section, that equation is not valid because steel stress is below 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>. Use strain compatibility there. The classification by A<sub>st</sub> against A<sub>st,lim</sub> avoids this trap.

IS 456 design practice keeps sections under-reinforced. An under-reinforced beam deflects, cracks and gives warning before collapse. An over-reinforced beam can crush suddenly with little warning. Balanced is a limit, not a normal design target. If capacity is short, add compression steel as in Chapter 2.3 rather than make the section over-reinforced. Design aids in Chapter 2.5 tabulate pt,lim.

figure.caption: Strain compatibility gives the neutral axis; comparing x<sub>u</sub> with x<sub>u,max</sub> gives the failure mode. For the worked example x<sub>u,max</sub> = 230 mm and A<sub>st</sub> = 2500 mm² is above A<sub>st,lim</sub> = 1713.1 mm².

spec.aria: Flowchart from strain compatibility to neutral axis depth, then three branches for under-reinforced, balanced and over-reinforced sections.

examples.question: A singly reinforced rectangular beam has b = 300 mm, d = 500 mm, f<sub>ck</sub> = 30 N/mm², f<sub>y</sub> = 500 N/mm² and A<sub>st</sub> = 2500 mm². Compute A<sub>st,lim</sub>, p<sub>t,lim</sub> and p<sub>t</sub>, and classify the section.
steps: For Fe500, x<sub>u,max</sub>/d = 0.46. So x<sub>u,max</sub> = 0.46 × 500 = 230 mm.
At the balanced condition, C = T: 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u,max</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st,lim</sub>.
A<sub>st</sub> = 2500 mm² > A<sub>st,lim</sub> = 1713.1 mm², and p<sub>t</sub> = 1.667% > p<sub>t,lim</sub> = 1.142%. The section is over-reinforced.
examples.answer: A<sub>st,lim</sub> = 1713.1 mm², p<sub>t,lim</sub> = 1.142%, p<sub>t</sub> = 1.667%; the section is over-reinforced.
examples.check:
b = 300.0
d = 500.0
fck = 30.0
fy = 500.0
Ast = 2500.0
xumax_ratio = 0.46
xumax = xumax_ratio * d
C = 0.36 * fck * b * xumax
Ast_lim = C / (0.87 * fy)
pt_lim = 100.0 * Ast_lim / (b * d)
pt = 100.0 * Ast / (b * d)
print(round(Ast_lim, 1))
print(round(pt_lim, 3))
print(round(pt, 3))
print(round(xumax, 1))

traps: Calling a section under-reinforced because A<sub>st</sub> is small, without comparing A<sub>st</sub> with A<sub>st,lim</sub> or x<sub>u</sub> with x<sub>u,max</sub>.
Using x<sub>u,max</sub>/d = 0.48 for Fe500 steel instead of 0.46.
Comparing p<sub>t</sub> with a fixed 1% or 0.75% instead of p<sub>t,lim</sub> for the actual f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>y</sub>.
Using 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub>b x<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>st</sub> to find x<sub>u</sub> for an over-reinforced section, where steel has not yielded.
Confusing overall depth D with effective depth d when computing p<sub>t</sub>.

quiz.a: A balanced section has x<sub>u</sub> = x<sub>u,max</sub>; concrete crushing and steel yielding begin together.

quiz.q: Why does a smaller x<sub>u</sub> make steel yield first?
quiz.a: From ε<sub>s</sub> = 0.0035(d − x<sub>u</sub>)/x<sub>u</sub>, a smaller x<sub>u</sub> gives a larger ε<sub>s</sub>, so steel reaches yield strain earlier.

quiz.q: For Fe415 and d = 450 mm, find x<sub>u,max</sub>.
A beam with f<sub>ck</sub> = 30 N/mm² and f<sub>y</sub> = 500 N/mm² has p<sub>t</sub> = 1.0%. Classify it.
quiz.a: p<sub>t,lim</sub> = 1.142%. Since p<sub>t</sub> < p<sub>t,lim</sub>, the section is under-reinforced.

quiz.q: Why does IS 456 design keep beams under-reinforced?
quiz.a: An under-reinforced beam gives ductile warning before collapse; an over-reinforced beam can crush suddenly.

quiz.q: b = 250 mm, d = 400 mm, f<sub>ck</sub> = 25 N/mm², f<sub>y</sub> = 415 N/mm², A<sub>st</sub> = 1100 mm². Compute p<sub>t</sub> and p<sub>t,lim</sub>.
Why is 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub>b x<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>st</sub> unsafe for an over-reinforced section?
quiz.a: Steel stress is below 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>. Using 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> in place of f<sub>s</sub> overestimates x<sub>u</sub>, so the depth obtained is wrong even though the classification may happen to come out right. Judge the section by comparing A<sub>st</sub> with A<sub>st,lim</sub>, or solve x<sub>u</sub> by strain compatibility.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern performance-based design uses curvature ductility and plastic hinge rotation, not only a section classification. Finite element models track cracking and steel yielding. Researchers search terms: tension-controlled section, compression-controlled section, curvature ductility, IS 456 x<sub>u,max</sub>. Newer codes may use different strain limits.
